rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient that should elute all 6 compounds without truncation and reveal the overall elution window and any critical pairs. The wide phi range and moderate slope give a good first map for later window trimming, slope, and temperature optimization.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is now to cut time while keeping every peak inside the gradient. The first run suggests the elution window is roughly phi 0.14 to 0.50, so a narrower window with a shorter gradient should speed the run substantially while still leaving margin for the last peak.

Resolution still has huge margin, so push further on speed by slightly narrowing the window and shortening the gradient. This should test how close we can get the last peak to 10 minutes while keeping all pairs comfortably above 1.5.

Since all pairs remain far above the resolution threshold, use temperature to trim retention without changing the gradient geometry. A 5 C increase should pull the last peak below 10 minutes and may reach the maximum CRF while preserving ample separation.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so now probe whether a faster method can still keep all adjacent pairs at or above 1.5 and the last peak under 10 minutes. The current method has large resolution margin, so a shorter, slightly narrower gradient is the logical next stress test.

Resolution margin is still very large and the last peak remains comfortably under 10 minutes, so push one more step toward a steeper, faster method. This tests whether we can further compress the run while keeping the weakest pair above the 1.5 threshold.

The 4 minute gradient was fast enough on the early peaks but too low in phi1, leaving the last compound in the hold and pushing t_last above 10 minutes. Raising phi1 one step while keeping tG at 4 minutes should bring the last peak back under 10 minutes, with resolution still likely ample.

The current 4 minute method already gives the maximum CRF, so use the extra budget to see if higher temperature can shorten the absolute run further without sacrificing the weakest pair. This also probes whether there is still hidden robustness margin around the current optimum.

The weakest pair is still above 1.5 at 50 C, so increase temperature one more step to find the resolution limit while maintaining the very fast 4 minute gradient. If pair 1-2 stays resolved, this confirms strong robustness; if not, 50 C is the clear upper edge.

At 55 C the first pair fell just below 1.5, so back off to 50 C but test a slightly narrower window to recover some selectivity while keeping the same short gradient. This checks whether the method can retain maximum CRF with a leaner window and may clarify how sensitive the critical early pair is to phi1 versus temperature.

We now know 4 minutes at 50 C is robust, so test the shortest possible gradient to see whether full resolution can still be maintained with the fastest program. The key question is whether the critical first pair remains above 1.5 under maximum gradient steepness.

The 2 minute gradient failed because the critical first pair compressed too much, so counter that by using both a slightly cooler temperature and a narrower window to recover early selectivity at the minimum tG. This directly tests whether 2 minutes can be made viable by trading some speed margin back into pair 1-2 resolution.

The limiting issue is pair 1-2 at high speed, while the last compound still stays under 10 minutes for several methods. Narrowing the window one more step at the proven 4 minute, 50 C condition should further improve the critical early-pair spacing by reducing gradient strength without needing to lengthen the run.

We have mapped the 4 minute method well, and the only unresolved boundary is whether the hottest setting can still keep the critical first pair at or above 1.5. This directly brackets the temperature ceiling around the fastest successful gradient.

Since higher temperature hurts the critical first pair, combine the hotter setting with the narrower window that improved pair 1-2 at 50 C. This should show whether 55 C can be rescued while still keeping the last peak under 10 minutes.

The 4 minute, 55 C, phi1 0.55 method still meets the resolution threshold, so test whether the hotter and narrower window can make the 2 minute gradient viable. This is the last plausible route to a still faster maximum-CRF method, with pair 1-2 again the decisive check.

The shortest viable gradient is clearly 4 minutes, so use the remaining budget to compare robustness at an only slightly longer but still maximum-CRF condition. This should show whether 6 minutes at 50 C offers a stronger safety margin on the critical first pair while keeping the last peak comfortably under 10 minutes.

A 4 minute gradient at 55 C and phi1 0.55 already achieved full score with the critical pair only just above threshold, so lengthening to 6 minutes should add robustness while still staying under 10 minutes. This checks whether a hotter, slightly longer method gives a strong reserve in pair 1-2 resolution without losing CRF.

Injection 18 shows phi1 0.55 at 6 minutes is just slightly too weak at 55 C, so lowering temperature one step should bring the last peak back under 10 minutes while preserving strong resolution. This fills in a useful robustness point around the 6 minute, narrower-window region.

The first pair is always the limiting one, and all early peaks are still retained enough that a modest increase in phi0 may reshape the front of the gradient without risking unretained elution. This tests whether shifting the window upward can preserve pair 1-2 while giving an even leaner fast method.

Injection 20 improved the fast method while keeping the critical pair comfortably above 1.5, so test whether the higher phi0 also stabilizes that pair at 55 C. This could identify an even faster high-temperature maximum-CRF variant if pair 1-2 remains resolved.

The shifted window at phi0 0.10 rescued the 55 C method with the critical pair still above 1.5, so the next step is to test whether it also rescues 60 C. This directly probes the hottest possible maximum-CRF condition on the fastest successful gradient.

The best fast condition so far is right on the edge at phi0 0.10, phi1 0.60, 4 minutes, 55 C with pair 1-2 at R 1.53. Raising phi0 one more step may further ease the critical early-pair compression while keeping the run very short, and it tests whether the front of the window can be shifted higher without creating near-unretained elution.

The best current fast method at 55 C is phi0 0.10, phi1 0.60, but it sits close to the resolution boundary for pair 1-2. Lowering phi1 one step should strengthen that critical separation while still likely keeping the last peak under 10 minutes, giving a potentially more robust maximum-CRF option.

For the final injection, map the most robust-looking fast window at a slightly cooler temperature to maximize margin on the critical first pair while preserving full score. This gives a cleaner robustness comparison against the hotter 55 C version and may identify the best practical choice among the many CRF-tied methods.
